directions.description: Gödel showed self-reference breaks completeness, but what if self-referential proofs are not paradoxes but VALID mathematical objects? Develop a proof theory where proofs can reference their own structure — a proof of theorem T can contain a subproof that assumes T as a hypothesis, forming a circular dependency that is resolved through a fixed-point construction. Conjecture: Non-well-founded proofs form a convergent fixed point under a natural topolog: the space of proof trees with the tree topology is a Scott domain, and self-referential proofs correspond to infinite chains whose lub is a valid proof. A proof that references itself is like a recursive function: it converges if the self-reference occurs at a strictly smaller ordinal. Test: formalize non-well-founded proof trees as coinductive types in Lean 4, prove that the proof of 'P implies P' by assuming P is a valid non-well-founded proof with ordinal height 1, and show that the liar sentence 'this statement is unprovable' is NOT a valid non-well-founded proof because its ordinal height is undefined. Impact: turns the liar paradox from a bug into a feature — self-referential proofs are a new class of mathematical object with their own consistency conditions.
directions.proof_strategy: Define NWFP (non-well-founded proofs) as coinductive types: a proof is a tree where children are proofs, but cycles are allowed as long as each cycle has decreasing ordinal rank. Define ordinal height: oh(P) = sup{oh(Q)+1 : Q is a subproof of P}. A NWFP is valid if oh(P) is a well-defined ordinal. Prove consistency: if NWFP proves False, then oh(False) < oh(False), contradiction. Prove completeness: every true Pi_1 sentence has a NWFP of finite height. Test: formalize in Lean 4 and verify the P-implies-P example.
directions.title: Non-Well-Founded Proofs: Proofs That Reference Themselves

directions.description: The integers Z live on a line, but what happens to arithmetic on a curved space? Define hyperbolic integers Z_H as the set of points in the Poincaré disk that are images of Z under a discrete subgroup Gamma of PSL(2,R). Define hyperbolic primes as the vertices of the tessellation induced by Gamma, and hyperbolic addition/multiplication via the group action. Conjecture: Z_H has unique factorization into hyperbolic primes, and the hyperbolic prime number theorem holds: the number of hyperbolic primes in a hyperbolic disk of radius R is asymptotic to R^2 / (2 log R). The hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum_{n in Z_H, |n|_H > 0} 1/|n|_H^{2s} satisfies a functional equation and has zeros only on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. Test: compute zeta_H(s) for the modular group Gamma = PSL(2,Z) and verify that the first 100 zeros lie on Re(s) = 1/2. Impact: number theory on curved spaces — where primes are geometric objects and the Riemann Hypothesis might be PROVABLE.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Z_H as the orbit of 0 under Gamma = PSL(2,Z) acting on the Poincaré disk. Define |n|_H as the hyperbolic distance from the origin. Prove Z_H is a discrete subset of the disk. Define the hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum 1/|n|_H^{2s} and prove it converges for Re(s) > 1. Prove the functional equation zeta_H(s) = pi^{s-1/2} Gamma((1-s)/2)/Gamma(s/2) zeta_H(1-s) using Selberg's trace formula. Test: compute first 100 zeros numerically and verify Re(s) = 1/2.
directions.title: Hyperbolic Number Theory: Arithmetic on the Poincaré Disk

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers are the largest ordered field, containing every real number and infinitely many infinities and infinitesimals. But what if a surreal number could be in SUPERPOSITION — simultaneously equal to multiple values until observed? Define quantum surreal numbers as surreal-valued quantum states: |psi> = sum_i alpha_i |No_i> where No_i are surreal numbers and alpha_i are complex amplitudes. Conjecture: The quantum surreal field Q(No) is a non-Archimedean quantum field where the spectral theorem extends: every self-adjoint operator on a quantum surreal Hilbert space has a spectral decomposition into surreal-valued projections. The key insight is that infinitesimal surreal numbers provide a natural framework for quantum measurement: the probability of observing |No_i> is not alpha_i^2 (which may be infinitesimal) but the standard part of alpha_i^2. Test: construct the quantum surreal number |psi> = (1/sqrt(2))|0> + (1/sqrt(2))|epsilon> where epsilon is an infinitesimal surreal, and prove that measuring |psi> gives 0 with probability st(1/2) = 1/2 and epsilon with probability st(1/2 * epsilon^2) = 0 — the infinitesimal is unobservable! Impact: a mathematical framework where quantum mechanics and non-Archimedean analysis meet, giving infinitesimal probabilities a rigorous treatment.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Q(No) as the tensor product of the surreal field No with the complex numbers C. Define quantum surreal Hilbert space H_Q(No) as the completion of Q(No)^n with respect to the surreal-valued inner product. Prove the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators on H_Q(No) by transfinite induction on the birthday of the surreal eigenvalues. The key lemma: if A is self-adjoint with surreal eigenvalues, then A = integral lambda dE(lambda) where E(lambda) are projections and lambda ranges over surreal numbers up to the birthday of A. Test: construct the 2x2 example and verify measurement probabilities.
directions.title: Quantum Surreal Numbers: Superposition of All Real Numbers

directions.description: Zero-knowledge proofs let you convince someone a statement is true without revealing WHY. Apply this to mathematics: a zero-knowledge proof of a theorem T convinces the verifier that T is provable in PA without revealing any step of the proof. Conjecture: Every theorem provable in Peano Arithmetic has a zero-knowledge proof whose communication complexity is polynomial in the length of the theorem statement (not the proof). This follows from the PCP theorem combined with the fact that PA-proofs can be arithmetized. The zero-knowledge protocol: (1) Prover commits to each proof step using a collision-resistant hash. (2) Verifier randomly challenges one proof step. (3) Prover opens that step and shows it follows from the axioms. Repeating O(k) times gives soundness error 2^{-k}. The proof is zero-knowledge because the verifier only sees one random step per challenge. Test: implement a zero-knowledge proof system for propositional tautologies and prove that a verifier learns nothing beyond the validity of the tautology. Impact: mathematicians can certify results without revealing their methods — a mathematical equivalent of sealed-bid auctions for proof strategies.
directions.proof_strategy: Arithmetize PA-proofs: encode each proof step as a polynomial equation over a finite field F_p. Apply the PCP theorem: every NP statement has a probabilistically checkable proof of constant query complexity. Convert the PCP to zero-knowledge using the Fiat-Shamir heuristic: the prover commits to the PCP oracle, the verifier sends a random challenge, and the prover responds with a proof that is zero-knowledge by the hiding property of the commitment. Prove soundness: a cheating prover must fool the verifier with probability at most 2^{-k}. Prove zero-knowledge: the simulator can generate indistinguishable transcripts without the proof. Test: implement for propositional resolution proofs of length up to 1000.
directions.title: Zero-Knowledge Theorem Proving: I Can Prove Fermat's Last Theorem Without Showing You the Proof

directions.description: Borges' Library of Babel contains every possible 410-page book — approximately 25^{1312000} volumes. The library is finite but vast beyond comprehension. Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. Conjecture: The probability that a random volume contains a meaningful proof of a given theorem T is approximately |T| * 25^{-k} where |T| is the length of T and k is the proof complexity of T. Moreover, the Library contains a universal catalog — a single volume that encodes the location of every other volume — and this catalog can be found in polynomial time using a variant of the de Bruijn sequence construction. The deepest question: does the Library contain its own complete catalog? By a diagonal argument, no single volume can encode all volumes (since 25^{1312000} > 1312000 * log_2(25^{1312000})). But a DISTRIBUTED catalog spanning N volumes can encode the entire Library if N > 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_2(25)). Test: compute the exact probability of finding a valid Lean 4 proof of a specific theorem in the Library. Construct a de Bruijn-based catalog for a mini-Library with alphabet size 4 and book length 16. Impact: the mathematics of universal information spaces — every possible text exists, but finding meaning requires a guide.
directions.proof_strategy: Define B = {0,...,24}^{1312000} as the Library. Compute |B| = 25^{1312000}. Define the meaning probability P(T) = sum_{b in B: b contains proof of T} 1/|B|. Prove P(T) >= |T| * 25^{-k(T)} where k(T) is the Kolmogorov complexity of T. Construct a distributed catalog using de Bruijn sequences: encode each volume's address as a substring of a de Bruijn sequence B(25, m) for m = ceil(log_{25}(1312000)). Prove the catalog requires N >= 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_{25}(2)) volumes. Test: implement the mini-Library with alphabet 4, book length 16, and compute meaning probabilities.
directions.title: The Library of Babel: Combinatorics of the Universal Library

directions.description:
# Future Directions — Congruence Rigidity of Sums of Squares

This cycle established that the entries of an integer right triangle are forced into
strong divisibility patterns — one leg is a multiple of three, the legs jointly carry a
factor of four, one entry is a multiple of five — and that a four-dimensional right
"box" (a solution of `a² + b² + c² = d²`) is even more rigid: at most one of its three
spatial edges can be odd. We also pinned down exactly which whole numbers can serve as a
leg. These findings point to several bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. The correct modulus for a power of two grows with the power
**Conjecture.** In any solution of `a² + b² = c²`, the two-adic valuation of the leg
product `a·b` is governed one level deeper than naive reduction suggests: deciding
whether `2^k` divides `a·b` is a question about residues modulo `2^{k+1}`, never modulo
`2^k`.
*The key insight is* that a difference of two odd squares is always divisible by eight,
so each additional factor of two in the product must be certified one binary place
further out than one would guess. *Why now?* Having isolated the exact `mod 8`
obstruction behind the factor of four, we can test the pattern mechanically for `k = 3,
4, 5` and either confirm a clean "shift-by-one" law or expose its first exception.

## 2. A universal super-divisor for higher-dimensional right figures
**Conjecture.** For every dimension `r`, solutions of `x₁² + ⋯ + x_r² = y²` obey a single
universal divisibility law: there is a constant `D(r)`, depending only on `r`, such that
`D(r)` divides the product `x₁·x₂·⋯·x_r` for *every* solution, and `D(r)` is the largest
such constant.
*The key insight is* that reduction to a finite residue ring turns "for all solutions"
into a finite, decidable statement, so the optimal constant `D(r)` is computable and
should grow in a structured (conjecturally multiplicative-over-primes) way. *Why now?*
The three-dimensional case already yields `4 ∣ x₁x₂x₃`; comparing it against the planar
constant `12` suggests a dimension-indexed sequence worth charting and predicting.

## 3. Parity collapse in higher dimensions
**Conjecture.** As the number of squared terms increases, the number of edges permitted to
be odd stays uniformly bounded: in `x₁² + ⋯ + x_r² = y²` at most three of the `x_i` can be
odd, regardless of `r`.
*The key insight is* that the sum of squares equals the count of odd terms modulo four,
while a perfect square is `0` or `1` modulo four, capping the admissible odd-count no
matter how many terms are added. *Why now?* We proved the cap is "at most one" in three
dimensions; extending the modular bookkeeping to arbitrary `r` is a self-contained next
step that would reveal whether the cap is truly dimension-independent.

## 4. A sharp threshold characterization of legs in every dimension
**Conjecture.** Just as the whole numbers that are a leg of a right triangle are exactly
those `≥ 3`, in each higher dimension there is a sharp finite threshold above which every
integer appears as an edge of some right figure, and the finitely many exceptions can be
listed explicitly.
*The key insight is* that a single explicit construction, split according to the parity of
the target edge, realizes all sufficiently large values, while the small exceptions are
forced by a factorization that would otherwise require a vanishing edge. *Why now?* The
planar threshold `3` and its sharpness (the failures at `1` and `2`) give a template that
should transfer verbatim to the box equation and beyond.

## 5. Divisibility as a sieve against near-solutions
**Conjecture.** The combined congruence obstructions (`12 ∣ a·b`, `60 ∣ a·b·c`, and their
higher-dimensional analogues) are strong enough that a random integer triple satisfying
them has a positive, computable probability of being genuinely Pythagorean — i.e. the
congruence conditions capture a constant fraction of the "arithmetic mass" of true
solutions.
*The key insight is* that each universal divisor removes a fixed proportion of impostors,
so stacking independent prime-power obstructions multiplies into a sieve of predictable
density. *Why now?* With the exact obstructions in hand for the primes `2, 3, 5`, one can
immediately measure how much of the solution set they explain and calibrate whether a few
more primes suffice to pin down solutions almost completely.
directions.title: That the entries of an integer right triangle are forced

If there exists a vertex coloring c : V → Colors such that for every vertex v, c(v) equals the weighted blend of the colors of its out‑neighbors (i.e., c(v) = π_{(u,p)∈Out(v)} p·c(u) ), then c must be constant. M(t) = (1‑ t^{d₁+1})(1‑ t^{d₂+1})(1‑ t^{d₃+2}) /

Prove non‑≥negativity of m_j (e.g., by interpreting them as Kostka numbers). 5. Use the known fact that Sym^j(u_SL₂) has a single Jordan block of size j+1 to conclude that π_λ(u) has Jordan blocks of size j+1 with multiplicities m_j.

directions.description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a phantom topology as a function T: O -> Top(X) from a set of observers to topologies on X. Define the intersection topology T_cap = intersection of all T(o). Prove: every second-countable T_0 space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with |O| = 2. Proof: for a basis {B_n}, define T(o1) as the topology generated by {B_n : n odd} union {X} and T(o2) by {B_n : n even} union {X}. Then T_cap = tau. Prove non-metrizable spaces need >= 3 observers: the Zariski topology on R^2 cannot be written as the intersection of two first-countable topologies. Test: verify the R example and construct the 3-observer phantom representation for the Zariski topology.
directions.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them

directions.description: A vampire number is a composite number v with an even number of digits that can be factizedd as v = x * y where x and y together have the same digits as v. The smallest is 1260 = 21 * 60. But vampire numbers are just the beginning. Define: (1) Werewolf numbers: v = x * y where x and y share exactly one digit with v. (2) Ghost numbers: v = x * y where v has NO digits in common with x or y. (3) Zombie numbers: v = x * y where x and y are both prime (these violate the definition but exist — 125460 = 204 * 615 = 246 * 510, where both factorizations involve a prime and a composite). Conjecture: The density of vampire numbers in [10^{2n}, 10^{2n+1}] approaches 1/sqrt(n) as n -> infinity. Every even-length interval [10^{2k}, 10^{2k+2}] contains at least one vampire number. Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.
directions.proof_strategy: Define vampire numbers formally: v is a vampire number iff v has 2n digits and there exist x, y each with n digits such that v = x*y and the multiset of digits of v equals the union of digits of x and y. Count the number of digit arrangements: for a 2n-digit number with distinct digits, there are C(2n, n) * n! * n! possible fang pairs, so the expected number of fang pairs is C(2n, n) * (n!)^2 / 10^{2n} = C(2n,n) / 10^n ~ 1/sqrt(n). Prove existence in every interval by constructing explicit vampire numbers using the formula 1260 * 10^{2k} for k >= 0. Test: enumerate up to 10^8.
directions.title: Vampire Numbers and Other Numerical Monsters: A Bestiary of Arithmetic Oddities

directions.description: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) and converges to the golden ratio. Define the ANTI-Fibonacci sequence: A(n+1) is the smallest positive integer that is NOT equal to A(n) + A(n-1). The sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ... (each term avoids being the sum of the two previous terms). Conjecture: The anti-Fibonacci sequence A(n) grows as A(n) ~ n^2/4, and the ratio A(n)/n^2 converges to 1/4. More precisely, A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1). The sequence avoids the golden ratio entirely — the ratio A(n+1)/A(n) does NOT converge, instead oscillating between 1 and 2. The complement of the anti-Fibonacci sequence (numbers that ARE sums of two previous anti-Fibonacci numbers) has density 0. Test: compute A(n) for n up to 10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 approaches 1/4. Prove A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1) by induction. Impact: a beautiful counterpoint to the Fibonacci sequence — instead of converging to a constant, it grows quadratically while systematically avoiding addition.
directions.proof_strategy: Define A(1) = A(2) = 1, A(n+1) = smallest positive integer not equal to A(n) + A(n-1). Prove by strong induction: A(n) >= floor(n^2/4). Base: A(1)=1 >= 0, A(2)=1 >= 1. Inductive step: if A(k) >= floor(k^2/4) for k <= n, then A(n) + A(n-1) >= floor(n^2/4) + floor((n-1)^2/4), so A(n+1) <= A(n) + A(n-1) - 1 + delta where delta accounts for gaps, giving A(n+1) >= floor((n+1)^2/4). Prove A(n) <= ceil(n^2/4) + 1 by showing the avoidance constraint only blocks one value per step. Test: compute A(n) for n=1..10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 -> 1/4.
directions.title: The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence: Numbers That Avoid the Golden Ratio at All Costs

directions.description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.
directions.proof_strategy: Define an Escher staircase in ring R as a strictly ascending chain I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... such that intersection of I_n is contained in I_1. Prove Int(Z) has an Escher staircase: I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z}. Each I_n is strictly contained in I_{n+1} (the polynomial x choose n is in I_{n+1} but not I_n). Intersection of I_n = {0} contained in I_1. Prove k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n: the chain (x_1) contained in (x_1,x_2) contained in ... contained in (x_1,...,x_n) has length n. Prove Z_p has no Escher staircase (Noetherian). Test: verify for Int(Z) and k[x,y,z].
directions.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back

directions.description: Deja vu — the feeling that you've experienced something before — is a fixed point in a dynamical system. Model cognitive state as a function f: S -> S mapping current brain state to next brain state. A deja vu is a state s such that f^n(s) = s for some n > 0 — a periodic point of the cognitive dynamical system. Conjecture: By Sharkovsky's theorem, the existence of a period-3 orbit in the cognitive dynamics (three distinct states that cycle) implies chaos in the sense of Li-Yorke, meaning there exist uncountably many cognitive trajectories that are neither periodic nor convergent. Moreover, the set of deja vu states (periodic points of f) is dense in the cognitive state space S if f is continuous and S is an interval. The frequency of deja vu (occurring in ~70% of people) corresponds to the natural density of periodic points in a typical chaotic map. Test: model cognitive dynamics as a logistic map f(x) = rx(1-x) on [0,1] with parameter r chosen to match empirical deja vu frequencies. For r = 3.83 (period-3 window), compute the density of periodic points and compare to the 70% lifetime incidence. Impact: deja vu is not a glitch — it's a mathematical inevitability of continuous cognitive dynamics. Any continuous cognitive map with a period-3 orbit MUST have deja vu.
directions.proof_strategy: Model cognitive state space as S = [0,1] and cognitive dynamics as f: S -> S continuous. Apply Sharkovsky's theorem: if f has a point of period 3, then f has points of all periods. A deja vu state is a periodic point: s such that f^n(s) = s. Prove: the set of periodic points is dense in S for the logistic map at r = 3.83. Compute the density of periodic points: PeriodicPoints_n(f) / n approaches the topological entropy h(f) as n -> infinity. For the logistic map at r = 3.83, h(f) ~ 0.38. The lifetime incidence of deja vu (~70%) is consistent with the probability that a random orbit encounters a periodic point neighborhood within a typical observation window. Test: simulate 10000 random orbits of the logistic map and count how many encounter periodic neighborhoods.
directions.title: The Mathematics of Deja Vu: Fixed Points in Consciousness and Cognition
